name: trealla-prolog
desc: Compact and efficient ISO Prolog interpreter written in plain old C
why: A compact ISO Prolog in plain C is a genuinely old-school logic language worth an afternoon of queries and backtracking.

brief.what_it_is: Trealla Prolog is a compact ISO Prolog interpreter written in plain C99 and built with a plain Makefile. You give it Prolog source files or queries, either on the command line with tpl or at its REPL, and it runs them and prints answers. The README also lists a C embedding API (libtrealla.a and trealla.h), a WebAssembly build, and a Python bridge marked experimental. The feature list covers unbounded integers and rationals, UTF-8 atoms and strings, DCGs, freeze/dif/when, CLP(B) and CLP(Z), tabling, threads, engines, actors, sockets, and SQLite via an FFI-backed module.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a compact, efficient ISO Prolog interpreter that runs on very many platforms, including bare boards and bare metal. It is also meant to be embeddable from C and usable in Jupyter notebooks.
brief.how_it_works: Trealla runs as a single tpl executable that loads files, consults .pl sources, and drops into a REPL with history when given no goal. Double-quoted text defaults to a packed UTF-8 byte array that behaves like a char list, and open/4 with mmap(Ls) gives a memory-mapped file view as a string. Tabling memoizes each call variant so left-recursive predicates terminate, and the table can be declared incremental or mode-directed (min/max).

brief.install_notes: On macOS and Linux, brew install trealla-prolog is enough; Apple Silicon and Linux (both architectures) get prebuilt bottles. An Intel Mac has no bottle and builds from source. Building from source needs a C99 compiler and make; on Debian-like systems the README lists build-essential, git, libedit-dev, libffi-dev and libssl-dev, and on macOS brew install libffi openssl coreutils. Optional make test wants a UTF-8 locale; the Makefile picks C.UTF-8 or en_US.UTF-8 if available. On first run tpl reads ~/.tplrc unless -f is given, and the library path defaults to a location relative to the executable or can be set with TPL_LIBRARY_PATH or --library.
brief.standout: The same binary covers a lot of ground for a small interpreter: tabling with incremental and mode-directed declarations, delimited continuations, engines and actors, and a freestanding profile that boots on a Raspberry Pi 4 and an Arduino Nano ESP32 with no operating system. Its strings are packed UTF-8 that behave like lists, and mmap'd files can be consumed as Prolog strings.
brief.status: The README says Trealla has reached a stable state and is feature-complete as far as planned, with only bug fixes and incremental improvements ongoing. The fetched text shows no release date or last commit, so current activity could not be verified from it.
brief.caveats: Unbounded integers are for arithmetic only and raise type_error when used elsewhere; the README also notes that printing very large bigints (100K+ digits) becomes exponentially slower because of the imath library. Several items are marked EXPERIMENTAL: rational trees, GSL and PLplot FFIs, and the bi-directional Python interface (Janus). The Raspberry Pi 4 port is described as a proof of concept with no interrupts, no filesystem, and no memory protection. Some tests differ under the C locale for accented text. Intel Macs have no bottle and must build from source. Windows and 32-bit Linux are cross-compiled rather than native. The README does not mention a licence in the fetched text, but the repository headline says MIT licensed.

entry.title: Trealla Prolog
entry.tldr: A compact ISO Prolog interpreter in plain C that gives you logic programming, tabling and constraint solving from one small tpl binary.
entry.deeper_look:
Trealla Prolog is an ISO Prolog interpreter written in C99 and built with a plain Makefile. You run `tpl` with source files or a goal, or start it with no goal and get a REPL with history. Prolog programs state facts and rules, then you ask questions and the engine searches for answers by backtracking.

The README describes it as a compact, efficient interpreter that runs on very many platforms, including bare boards and bare metal. The feature list is long for something small: unbounded integers and rationals, UTF-8 atoms and strings, DCGs, freeze/dif/when, CLP(B) and CLP(Z) constraint solvers, threads, engines, actors, sockets, and SQLite through an FFI-backed module. It can also be embedded in C programs, built to WebAssembly, and used from Jupyter.

The idea underneath is declarative programming. Tabling memoizes each call variant, so left-recursive predicates that would loop forever in plain Prolog terminate. Tables can be declared incremental or mode-directed (min/max). Double-quoted text is a packed UTF-8 byte array that behaves like a char list, and a file opened with mmap can be read as a Prolog string. This gives you a small, readable system for exploring how logic languages work.
entry.install:
brew install trealla-prolog
# Apple Silicon and Linux get prebuilt bottles; an Intel Mac builds from source.
# Depends on openssl; building by hand needs a C99 compiler and make.

Starts the REPL with history, where you can consult files and type queries.

entry.whats_unique: One small C binary covers tabling, delimited continuations, engines, actors and constraint solving. It also has a freestanding profile that boots on a Raspberry Pi 4 and an Arduino Nano ESP32 with no operating system.
entry.caveats: Unbounded integers work for arithmetic only, rational trees, some FFIs and the Python bridge are marked experimental, and the Raspberry Pi bare-metal port is only a proof of concept.
